title: The icon wars
hookLine: emperors smashed icons; John of Damascus argued that since God became visible, he can be painted

lines: A LADDER AT THE PALACE GATE.
A CROWD AT THE FOOT OF IT.
cards: Workmen climb a ladder outside a palace gate in Constantinople. Above the gate hangs an image of Christ, and they've been sent to take it down.

Tradition says a crowd of ordinary people gathered at the foot of the ladder, some of them women, and shook it until the man on it fell. Whether every detail happened that way or not, the story shows what was at stake.
For a long stretch, on and off, Christians in the eastern empire fought over pictures: could a church hold images of Christ, of Mary, of the saints, or did they have to go?

teach.b: Iconoclasm means image-breaking, and an iconoclast is an image-breaker. Today it means anyone who smashes a tradition; here it was literal.
Some emperors ordered icons removed, plastered over or destroyed, and people who defended them were punished. Be fair to the iconoclasts.

teach.h: THOU SHALT NOT MAKE ANY GRAVEN IMAGE.
teach.b: Their argument came straight from scripture, the commandment in the King James Bible: "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image."
They worried that Christians were bowing to wood and paint, and that God, who has no body, can't be pictured at all. That was a serious worry, held by believers.

Then a monk named John, born in Damascus and living in a monastery near Jerusalem, outside the emperor's reach, wrote back. Once, he said in effect, God had no body and no face, so no one could make an image of him.

teach.h: JOHN: GOD HAS NOW BEEN SEEN.
teach.b: But now God has been seen. The Word became flesh. He walked, ate, wept, was touched.
So I paint what I have seen. I don't worship the wood, he said; I worship the maker of matter, who became matter for my sake.

teach.h: THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.
teach.b: Paul's letter to the Colossians gives him his key phrase: Christ is "the image of the invisible God."
If God has already made an image of himself, a human face, then a picture of that face isn't an insult to the invisible God. It says he really came. Christians still differ here.

Orthodox and Catholic Christians use icons and images in prayer. Some Protestant churches have pictures and crosses; some keep their walls deliberately plain, out of the same care for the commandment.
Each side is trying to honor the same God.

how: Orthodox and Catholic Christians pray with icons and images, often lighting a candle or kissing an icon; some Protestant churches keep images and crosses, and others keep their walls plain out of care for the commandment against graven images.

o: a rule that only kings may own holy images
image-breaking: removing or destroying holy pictures
the art of painting icons for prayer in churches

games.q: the icon wars — tap the pairs.
p: the image of the invisible God

s: they were believers who argued from the commandment against graven images.
John of Damascus said icons themselves should be worshiped
he said he worshiped not the matter, but its maker, who became matter.

games.q: you're John of Damascus. the emperor says pictures of Christ break the commandment. how do you answer?
o: God has now been seen in Christ, so I can paint what I've seen.
pictures are just decoration, so it doesn't matter.
games.why: John's case rests on the incarnation: the invisible God became visible, so his human face can be painted.

practice: Look at any image of Christ, an icon, a painting, a stained-glass window, and notice the face, the eyes, how its maker imagined him.
If you pray, let the image be a window rather than the point, and pray through it; if you don't, notice that someone painted this because they believed a face had been seen.

wordCard.voice: Iconoclasm. Image-breaking: the struggle in the eastern church over whether Christ and the saints could be pictured, and the name for smashing images.

orig.note: Greek: image, the word in "the image of the invisible God."

carryVoice: Your line: the invisible became visible. For John of Damascus, that settled it. Rest well.
